newsitem.title: USA: Expediency makes Clinton a micro-president.
newsitem.headline: Expediency makes Clinton a micro-president.

text.p: If ever there was a good illustration of Bill Clinton's micro-presidency, this is it: on April 27, Clinton will visit a Philadelphia neighbourhood to help its residents scrub away graffiti.

Clinton, hobbled politically by opposition control of Congress and a brace of scandals, and now temporarily hobbled physically by a knee injury, will take part in the cleanup push to kick off a domestic summit on volunteerism.

Cleansing walls and buildings of graffiti is hardly the kind of leadership the U.S. public saw in previous presidents, but budget constraints and political realities have combined to make Clinton a minimalist commander-in-chief.

Budget constraints mean there is no money for the kind of social activism that was the hallmark of Clinton's Democratic predecessors like Franklin Roosevelt and Lyndon Johnson, who respectively championed Social Security retirement benefits for the elderly and the now-largely abandoned War on Poverty.
Nor is there political support for such liberal activism, since conservative Republicans hold a majority in the Senate and House of Representatives.

"It's an interesting dilemma for a Democrat, the leader of a party that supposedly favours big government, to have to find new, inexpensive ways of addressing the country's problems," a White House official said.

Lending a hand in the community cleanup drive (along with wife Hillary and Vice President Al Gore and his wife Tipper) is Clinton's way of stressing that neighbour helping neighbour can do much to rid the United States of urban blight, he said.

Nowhere is Clinton's minimalist approach more obvious than in the field of health care reform. Though he came into office four years ago promising cradle-to-grave health care benefits for every American, the collapse of that effort in the face of a withering assault from the health insurance industry and its Republican allies has led him to seek only marginal reforms.

This week, for example, Clinton asked Congress to tighten screening of doctors who get Medicare and Medicaid payments to fight fraud and abuse, hardly a controversial proposal. He also appointed a 32-member commission to monitor health care quality and said he would try to ensure that Medicare, Medicaid and federal employee health plans follow the National Cancer Institute's recommendation that women in their 40's get mammograms to aid early detection of breast cancer.

In previous administrations, such moves probably would have been deemed too minor to merit presidential announcement. Clinton's focus on the mundane -- his second-term agenda also includes pushing for school uniforms and teenage curfews -- has grown more pronounced since Time magazine lampooned his leadership as "The Incredible Shrinking Presidency."
White House aides say Clinton, rather than involving himself in trivial pursuits, is showing he is in touch with the concerns of ordinary people.

So far the public seems to agree. Clinton's popularity in the polls is at the mid-50 percent level, about the same as Republican Ronald Reagan at this stage of his presidency. Reagan, like Clinton, won a second term in office.

But in "Behind the Oval Office," his insider book about Clinton's 1996 re-election drive, political consultant Dick Morris says Clinton realised that unless he did great things, historians were likely to rank him as a third-tier president.
Morris left the Clinton campaign in disgrace last August following the exposure of his affair with a prostitute.
